analysis.one_liner: Lets the government wiretap foreign calls without warrants and shield phone companies from lawsuits for helping.
analysis.headline: The Senate killed the surveillance bill 43-45 on its only day on the floor, short of the 60 votes the chamber had agreed it would need.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the 1978 foreign-surveillance law so that no court order is needed to tap calls and emails between people outside the United States, even when those communications pass through American networks. The Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence could start tapping immediately, then submit paperwork afterward, and could order phone and internet companies to cooperate. A court would check the government's procedures rather than approve specific targets, and companies that helped could not be sued.
analysis.who_benefits: The executive branch's intelligence agencies, which gain authority to conduct surveillance of foreign-to-foreign communications without per-target warrants and to compel telecom companies' assistance, and the telecommunications carriers, which would be paid at prevailing rates and shielded from lawsuits for that assistance.

how_it_helps.text: A court order would not be required for electronic surveillance of communications between people not located in the United States, even if the communication passes through the U.S. or the surveillance device is located here [S3][S2].

The Attorney General and Director of National Intelligence could authorize surveillance of people believed to be abroad immediately, filing a certification within five days and an application within ten, while the surveillance continued [S3].

The government could compel any communications provider to furnish information, facilities, and technical assistance; the provider would be compensated at prevailing rates and no cause of action would lie against anyone for providing that assistance [S3].

The bill did carry guardrails its supporters could point to: a 180-day sunset, Inspector General reports every four months, minimization procedures for U.S. persons approved by the court, and a requirement to shift to ordinary FISA warrants if surveillance turned to people inside the United States [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Americans' privacy. Anyone's international calls or emails that touch U.S. networks could be collected without a warrant targeting them, a court would approve the government's methods once for up to a year without applications naming specific targets or places, and the lawsuit shield would erase the main remedy people had against telecom companies that had already cooperated with the warrantless wiretapping program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Users of international communications touching U.S. networks

drawbacks.text: No court order would be required to tap communications between people outside the United States, even when those calls and emails route through American networks [S3][S2].

A court reviewing an application would assess the government's procedures, not specific targets — applications would not be required to identify the people, facilities, or places to be surveilled [S3].
The government could begin surveillance with no prior court order, and keep it running through review, extensions, and appeals [S3].

No lawsuit would lie against any person or company for providing information or assistance under a court order or government directive, removing judicial accountability for telecom cooperation with surveillance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was the more moderate of the FISA bills on the floor that week — it had a sunset, court review of procedures, minimization rules, and Inspector General reporting, which is why civil-liberties-minded Democrats could vote for it. But its core still loosens the warrant requirement FISA was built on, and its liability shield is the provision with the clearest cost to ordinary people: it would protect the companies whose cooperation with earlier warrantless spying was the subject of pending lawsuits. The national-security argument for speed on foreign-to-foreign taps is real; the immunity provision is hard to defend as anything other than a shield for past conduct.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate took it up by unanimous consent on August 3, 2007, under an order that passage would take 60 votes; it got 43 and lost 43-45, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S5][S6].

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin introduced the bill on August 3, 2007, for himself and Sen. Rockefeller, and the Senate considered it the same day [S1][S3][S5].
It failed passage 43-45, with the record noting it did not achieve the required 60 affirmative votes under the day's order; it was then placed on the Senate calendar [S5][S6].
The vote split fully by party: 42 of 49 Democrats and the one Independent voted yes, while all 43 voting Republicans voted no [S6].
The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings on September 25, 2007, but no vote ever followed [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senate Republicans and the White House, who opposed this version as too weak — and who got what they wanted days later, when Congress passed a broader FISA expansion with far fewer court safeguards. Telecom companies also came out ahead over time, since the stronger law that followed eventually gave them the retroactive immunity this bill only partially offered. The main immediate loser was the compromise position: court-checked surveillance without the liability shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Republicans and the White House; a stronger law followed

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it to the floor under unanimous consent on August 3, 2007.

for.name: Jay Rockefeller

for.what_they_did: Voted for the bill on the 43-45 roll call.

against.what_they_did: Every voting Republican opposed the bill, dooming it to fall short of the 60 votes required.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Publicly demanded that Congress expand FISA before the August recess and backed the stronger, court-light version Senate Republicans voted for instead of this compromise.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 43 voting Republicans voted no, while 42 of 49 Democrats voted yes — a clean party-line split, 43-45, with both sides having agreed the bill would need 60 votes to pass.

industries.note: The bill would make phone and internet companies the mandatory channel for government surveillance — compelled to assist, paid for it, and barred from being sued for it. Locking in their role and wiping out lawsuits over earlier warrantless-wiretapping cooperation comes directly at the expense of Americans' ability to hold those companies accountable in court [S3].

The bill would give the executive branch authority to surveil foreign-to-foreign communications through U.S. networks without per-target warrants, with immediate start authority and court review of procedures rather than specific targets. That gain in speed and reach is paid for in the privacy of ordinary people's international communications [S3][S2].
